passage: I am Farhan, and I still think about the day my bike chain snapped near the flyover. It was raining, I was already late, and a customer was calling every minute. I sat on the kerb feeling like the smallest person in the city. Then Naveen from the tea stall arrived with a spanner, and two others held an umbrella over my bag. That tea stall is where riders swap which lanes flood, which gates have rude guards, and who has spare parts. I feel like I belong there. Last month, after a week of long waits at restaurants, several of us wrote a short message to the platform asking for a fair waiting rule. No answer yet. But we wrote it together, and it felt good.

qa.q: Who arrived with a spanner when Farhan's chain snapped?
qa.a: Naveen from the tea stall arrived with a spanner.

qa.q: Why did Farhan feel like the smallest person in the city on the kerb?
qa.a: Farhan was alone in the rain, already late, with a broken bike and a customer calling every minute, so Farhan felt helpless.

qa.q: How could Farhan and the other riders use their network to improve their terms?
qa.a: They can keep sharing information, keep writing joint messages about waiting rules, and keep building trust so they speak together.

qa.q: How might Naveen see helping Farhan?
qa.a: Naveen probably sees it as normal among riders, since the group shares parts, routes and warnings. It shows the network works because people show up for each other.

grounding: Riders at the tea stall share routes and help with a broken bike, giving belonging, and use the network to ask for better terms together.

passage: The kebab kiosk near Warsaw's central station was where the riders waited between orders, and in his first winter Ivan learned more there than from the app. Amara, from Lagos, showed him which bridge iced over first. An older rider warned everyone about an address where a customer grabbed at bags. When Ivan's chain snapped at 10 p.m., three riders appeared with tools and a torch. He had moved from Kharkiv knowing nobody; now there was a place where people knew his name. One night, over cheap coffee, Amara said, 'We all lost the rain bonus this month. One complaint gets ignored. Thirty doesn't.' Ivan offered to set up a group chat and collect everyone's screenshots. By Sunday there were twenty-six riders in it and a draft letter to the company, polite and signed by all of them. Ivan read it twice and felt, for the first time in Poland, part of something.

qa.q: What does Ivan feel about the riders at the kiosk?
qa.a: Ivan feels grateful and at home, having come from Kharkiv knowing nobody and now having people who know his name.

qa.q: How did the riders use their network beyond helping each other?
qa.a: They collected screenshots and signed a polite joint letter to the company about the lost rain bonus.

qa.q: Why might Amara think thirty complaints matter more than one?
qa.a: Amara seems to have seen single complaints ignored, and believes a group is harder for the company to dismiss.

grounding: Shows riders sharing routes, warnings and repairs, the belonging it creates, and the network being used to ask for better terms together.

passage: In the waiting room of the grocery dark store in Pune, the riders kept a whiteboard nobody had officially allowed. Chetan had started it in his second month: 'Flooded: Sinhagad Road underpass', 'Dog pack: Lane 7', 'Customer at B-wing asks for OTP twice, be careful.' Suraj, the newest rider, read it on his first day and laughed. By his third day he was adding to it. When Suraj's tyre went flat in the monsoon, Chetan and two others found a spare tube and fixed it in the parking lot in ten minutes. Suraj felt, for the first time since leaving Latur, that he had people. Then the store cut the per-order rate. The riders gathered by the whiteboard. 'Nobody goes alone to the store manager,' Chetan said. 'We go together, with our order slips.' The next morning eighteen riders stood outside the manager's glass cabin, calm, slips in hand. The manager agreed to a meeting on Friday.

qa.q: What did the whiteboard say about Lane 7?
What did Suraj feel after the riders fixed his tyre?
qa.a: Suraj felt grateful and relieved, sensing he had people for the first time since leaving Latur.

qa.q: Why was going to the manager together wise?
qa.a: A calm group with order slips is harder to ignore than one rider, and nobody gets singled out.

qa.q: What might Chetan have wanted when he started the whiteboard?
qa.a: Chetan likely wanted riders to keep each other safe and informed, which later made standing together easier.

grounding: Shows riders at a dark store sharing warnings and help, a newcomer finding belonging, and the group going together to ask for better terms.
